limits.title: What the shooting percentage does not show
limits.description: A high percentage is not automatically good, a low one not automatically bad. Four things you have to think along with.

items.title: The number of shots
items.text: 100 per cent from one shot is worth less than 55 per cent from twenty. Whoever takes on the responsibility often has the more thankless percentage.

items.title: The quality of the chances
items.text: Someone who only finishes free counters has it easier than a back-court player against a closed block. Without the shot position, the percentage is only half the truth.

items.title: The match context
items.text: In the closing stages, short-handed or against the league leaders, percentages drop. That is normal and no sign of declining performance.

items.title: The development
items.text: A value from one match is a snapshot. Only the trend across several matches shows whether something is changing – upwards as well as downwards.

faq.description: Short answers to the questions that come up while calculating.

items.question: How do you calculate the shooting percentage in handball?
items.answer: You divide the goals by the shots and multiply by 100: shooting percentage (%) = goals ÷ shots × 100. Example: 7 goals from 12 shots make 58.3 per cent.

items.question: What counts as a shot?
items.answer: Every genuine attempt on goal: a goal, a saved ball, hitting the post or the bar and a clear miss. A turnover without an attempt – a travelling call, for instance – is not a shot and does not go into the percentage.

items.question: What is a good shooting percentage?
items.answer: It depends on the position. At the pivot 65–75 per cent counts as good, from the back court 45–55 per cent, from seven metres 75–85 per cent and on the fast break 85–95 per cent. A team shooting percentage above 60 per cent is solid in amateur handball.

items.question: How do I calculate the goalkeeper's save percentage?
items.answer: Save percentage = saves ÷ (saves + goals conceded) × 100. 14 saves from 30 shots on target make around 47 per cent. In amateur handball, values above 33 per cent count as strong and above 40 per cent as outstanding.

items.question: From how many shots is the percentage meaningful?
items.answer: As a rule of thumb: under ten shots the percentage is mostly chance. 100 per cent from one shot says less than 55 per cent from twenty. So always look at the number of attempts alongside it.

howTo.title: How to build your formation
howTo.description: The board does not start empty but with a 6:0 defence against a 3:3 attack. From there it is all dragging and tapping.

steps.title: Choose a formation
steps.text: A 6:0 against a 3:3 attack is already on the board. Below the court you can pick 5:1, 3:2:1, the 4:2 attack, the fast break or an empty court instead.

steps.title: Drag the magnets
steps.text: Push every magnet into place with a finger or the mouse. Orange is your team, blue the opposition, turquoise the goalkeeper. Double-tap or press and hold to open number, colour and delete right on the magnet – without taking your eyes off the court.

steps.text: In the tool rail – beside the court, above it on a phone – tap the arrow icon and then drag on the court from where to where. Start on a player and the arrow attaches to them. A single tap places an arrow of standard length. The middle handle bends it, the note icon puts a keyword beside it.

notes.title: 6:0 against 3:3
notes.text: The standard situation in amateur and youth handball: six defenders in one line at six metres, facing three back-court players, two wings and a pivot. If you want to discuss a screen or a crossing move, this is where you start.

notes.title: 5:1 with the advanced defender
notes.text: A five-man chain at the line, one player level with the free-throw line. On the board you see at once which space the advanced defender opens up – and where the attack can play around him.

notes.title: 3:2:1 in three rows
notes.text: Three players at six metres, two in front of them, one advanced at nine. The staggering is the whole point of this system, and staggering is hard to tell but easy to show.

notes.title: 4:2 with two pivots

limits.title: What a tactics board cannot do
limits.description: A drawn move always looks good – on the board nobody defends. Four things you have to think along with.

items.title: A board is a still image
items.text: A move is a sequence: screen, peel off, pass. A picture holds one moment of it. Draw two or three boards in sequence rather than squeezing every arrow into one.

items.title: The opposition does not stand still
items.text: The blue magnets stay exactly where you pushed them. A real defence shifts, helps out and switches. What looks free on the board is often free for half a second in the hall.

items.title: Formation is not execution
items.text: The positions are the easy part. Timing, pace and the pivot's read decide whether the same move ends as a goal or an offensive foul – and that is in no diagram.

items.title: Whether it worked, the board does not say
items.text: After the match the question remains whether the move really produced attempts and from which zones. Only an analysis answers that, not a drawing.

limits.closing: How to read out of a match whether the move carried is in the guide: <analysis>match analysis in handball: analysing matches properly</analysis>. items.question: How do I create a handball formation online?
items.answer: In the tactics board you choose a ready-made formation – 6:0, 5:1 or 3:2:1 for instance – and then drag the magnets into position. items.question: Is the tactics board free?
items.answer: Yes, entirely. There is no sign-up, no account, no time limit and no cap on how many boards you save or share. The PNG download and the share link work without an email address too.

items.question: Are my formations stored?
items.answer: No. The board runs entirely in your browser. When you tap “copy link”, the whole formation sits in the link itself – behind the hash. Browsers never send that part of an address to a server. So there is no database holding your tactics.

items.question: Are the court dimensions correct?
items.answer: Yes. The court is drawn to scale: 40 by 20 metres, the goal-area line 6 metres from the goal, the dashed free-throw line 9 metres, plus the seven-metre and goalkeeper restraining lines. The 6-metre line is built like the one in the hall, from two quarter circles at the posts and a straight section, not as a semicircle.

items.question: Does the tactics board work on a tablet in the hall?
items.answer: That is what it is built for. Every grab point is at least 44 pixels, there is nothing that needs a mouse, and the board runs in portrait as well as landscape. You open number and colour with a double tap or a long press right on the magnet. As long as the move tool is active you can scroll the page over the board as normal – only when drawing does the court take the gesture.

items.name: Live recording
items.headline: The sheet of paper that does the maths
items.summary: Record goals, shots, saves, suspensions and substitutions in real time – with a single tap, straight from the bench.
items.tagline: One tap per action. At the end of the match the statistic is finished, not the typing up.
intro: Live recording is the core of Statix. On screen your squad stands on the court, as on a tactics board. You tap the player who has just shot and pick the action — goal, saved, wide, blocked, post, seven metres, turnover, suspension. That was the whole procedure.

The app works out everything else: shooting percentage, attacking efficiency, save percentage, playing shares, goal difference, the flow of the match. You see them in the same second you need them — not on Sunday evening, when the sheet of paper has already vanished into the sports bag.

Because a match is faster than any input form, there is a quick mode for everything you have to tap without looking, and a guided mode for assistant coaches recording for the first time. Shot position and goal zone are two extra taps on a court graphic — not compulsory, but the precondition for the shot map.

steps.body: Tap the player, pick the action. The scorer list, the percentages and the flow of the match update at once — with the same tap that records the action.

steps.body: One tap on the court graphic fixes where the shot came from, a second one which corner of the goal. Both are optional: without the position only the shot map is missing, not a number.

steps.title: Straighten it out after the match
steps.body: Caught the wrong player, missed a save? Every recorded action can be changed or deleted afterwards, and all derived values recalculate.

There is no automatic detection from video. Every action comes from a person who saw it.

faq.question: How many taps is a match?
faq.answer: Roughly as many as the actions you want to record. Depending on the level, a handball match has 100 to 160 actions that move a statistic. Record only goals and shots and you tap correspondingly less — the percentages work with whatever is there.

faq.question: Can an assistant coach record who does not know the app?
faq.answer: Yes. The guided mode asks step by step instead of offering everything at once. That is enough for a first outing; after two matches almost everyone taps in quick mode.

faq.question: What happens if I mistap?
faq.answer: The last action can be undone immediately, any older one edited or deleted in the match log. All percentages and the shot map recalculate afterwards — there is no state that is “already saved” and therefore stays wrong.

faq.question: Do I need a tablet?
faq.answer: No. Statix runs on a phone just as it does on a tablet, iPad or laptop. A tablet is more comfortable because more of the squad is visible at once — necessary it is not.

items.headline: Built for halls with no signal
items.summary: Record matches offline in the hall with automatic synchronisation, and install Statix as an app on your home screen.
items.tagline: The hall has no signal. That is not a special case but the condition Statix was built under.
intro: Statix records a match entirely on the device. Every tap lands first in the browser's local storage and only afterwards — at some point, when there is a signal again — on the server. To you both look the same: the numbers are there at once, whether the bar at the top right shows a signal or not.

The way back is the actual point. When synchronising, the collected actions are played one after another against endpoints that recognise and discard an action sent twice. A signal that comes and goes three times therefore does not produce three goals.

Statix is installed as a PWA: “Add to Home Screen” on the iPhone, “Install app” in the Chrome menu. After that the app starts full screen without a browser bar, has an icon of its own and works in flight mode exactly as with a signal. No app store download is needed.

faq.answer: No. What is stored are events, not videos — a whole match is a few dozen kilobytes.

intro: The live ticker is the same recording, seen from outside. You release a match and get a link and a QR code. Whoever opens the link sees the score, the clock and the flow of the match in real time — every action appears there in the second you record it.

It is meant for the people who otherwise ask on WhatsApp: parents who are at work, the rest of the club, the second team playing at the same time. The QR code works on a sheet printed out and taped to the hall entrance just as well as on the projector at the club evening.

The ticker deliberately does not show everything. It shows what stands on a scoreboard — score, time, scorers, suspensions. The full statistic with percentages and shot map stays with you until you share it explicitly.

items.tagline: Every recorded action lands with a person. Out of that comes a season you can read.
intro: Live recording leaves a complete account for every player: goals, shots, shooting percentage, seven-metre throws counted separately, assists, turnovers, steals, blocks, suspensions. For goalkeepers, saves, goals conceded and save percentage.

It only gets interesting over time. Statix lays the matches of a season on top of one another and shows the curve — which percentage is rising, which is tipping over, who is a different player after the winter break. That is the number a training decision can carry, not the one shooting percentage from the one match.
Every number stays expandable down to the single action. Anyone who wants to know why a percentage stands at 38 % reaches the list of shots it was calculated from in two taps.

items.name: Shot maps & shot analysis
items.headline: Not how many, but from where
items.summary: Visualise shots and goals on the court and spot the patterns that decide matches.
items.tagline: A table says how many. A shot map says from where — and that is the question a training session comes out of.
intro: If you tap the shooting position along with the shot while recording, Statix draws the shot map from it: every shot a dot on the court, goal and miss distinguishable, condensed into a heat map. Next to it the second map, the goal zone — which corner was aimed at and what arrived there.

The use is not in the single dot, it is in the pattern. That you score from the left back position at nine metres and not from the right stands in no percentage; on the map you see it in two seconds. The same goes for the defensive side: where the opponent gets their shots away is a statement about your shifting.
There are shot maps for a single match, for one player across the season and for the team as a whole. The interesting comparison is usually the last one against the first.

steps.title: Cross it with the goal zone
steps.body: Where in the goal the balls land is the question for the opposing keeper — and for your own, when you look at the goals conceded.

steps.title: Translate it into training

items.name: AI analysis
items.headline: A second look at your numbers
items.summary: AI analyses for single matches, the whole team, individual players and complete tournaments – with pseudonymised player names.
items.tagline: The numbers are there anyway. The AI writes down what stands in them — and where they contradict each other.
intro: Statix sends the recorded match data through an analysis in four cuts: a single match, the whole team across the season, one player as a scouting profile, and a complete tournament. What comes out is not flowing prose but a report made of blocks — turning points, distribution of errors, shooting-zone efficiency, player performance, concrete starting points.

items.headline: A recording turns into a question
items.summary: Upload match recordings, tag scenes, filter by action and player, and send edits to individual players.
items.tagline: The recording is on the phone anyway. Tagged, it becomes a question you can ask: "every fast break against a 5-1".
intro: Video tagging is the workbench next to the statistic. You upload the recording of a match and lay scenes on top of it: shot, turnover, defensive action, save, suspension, game situation. Every scene is an interval in the video plus the note of what happened in it — and who.

Above the code lies a second layer: qualifiers. Out of which phase (positional attack, 1st/2nd/3rd wave, breakthrough), against which defence (6-0, 5-1, 3-2-1), with a player more or fewer, with which starting move, from which shooting position. That is why you can ask later: every wing shot against a 5-1 out of the second wave. The vocabulary is checked against the legend of an official IHF match report, not built from memory.

A playlist does not save a list of clips, it saves the question. Tag a forgotten scene later and it falls in by itself — nothing has to be put together a second time. The same mechanism carries the deliveries: a player receives exactly her scenes and does not see the rest of the match.

A tag moves no number. The statistic comes from live recording; tagged scenes are a reading of the video and do not change the list of scorers.

faq.question: Can I use video tagging today?
faq.answer: Only if your account is enabled for it. The function is being built right now and runs with a few teams who give feedback. Write to us if you want to be part of it — the waiting list is an e-mail.

faq.question: What is the difference between a tag and a recorded action?
faq.answer: A recorded action is the record of the match and feeds every statistic. A tag is an interval on the video with a reading. That is why you can tag a scene without any percentage changing — and why the workbench shows both side by side.

faq.question: Does a player see the whole match when I send her scenes?
faq.answer: No. A delivery serves only the pieces of the video her scenes cover. For everything else there is no address — not merely no button, but no reachable place.

faq.question: How much storage does a match need?
faq.answer: In 1080p roughly two to three gigabytes per match. In 4K a multiple of that, without anything more being visible on the workbench — hence the recommendation to film in 1080p.

The part that really changes everyday life is absences. Holiday, illness or an injury is entered once as a period and applies to every date inside it — including the one you only create tomorrow. Before, nobody declined nine training sessions one by one, so nobody declined at all.

On top come the small things everything otherwise hangs on: a deadline for answering with a reminder, push notifications when a date is added, moved or cancelled, and a calendar subscription that puts every date in your own phone calendar and keeps it current there.

faq.question: What happens if I move a date?

faq.question: Are all features included in the free access?

faq.answer: The feature is finished, but it is set up for you rather than created by you. That concerns the club area: what a club with two teams needs is not what a club with twelve needs.

faq.question: Do I have to use all of it?
